title: A 6–3 rate hold and a unanimous plan to unwind £368 billion of gilts
summary: September produced two distinct decisions. Six members kept Bank Rate at 3.75%, with Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill again preferring 4%. All nine agreed a multi-year plan to run down the remaining gilt portfolio held for monetary policy. An unchanged split on rates concealed an important change in the committee’s assessment: the risks to inflation had moved further upwards since July. The balance-sheet decision, by contrast, was designed to make future sales predictable enough that Bank Rate could remain the instrument used to adjust monetary conditions (minutes, paragraphs 18–33 and 44–48).

By 14 September Brent crude stood at $106 per barrel and UK wholesale gas at 207 pence per therm. Spot prices had approached levels in the adverse July scenario while futures further out remained lower than that scenario. The committee associated the rises with protracted Middle East conflict and energy disruption involving Russia and Ukraine. CPI inflation reached 3.1% in August. Direct energy effects, chiefly motor fuel, explained around 0.7 percentage points of the 1.1-point overshoot of target. Services inflation was 3.4%, down from 4.5% in March. With energy priced on 14 September, staff projected roughly 3¾% CPI inflation in the fourth quarter against July’s 3.2% forecast, and slightly above 4% early in 2027. This was a conditional update, dominated by the changed cost of energy (paragraphs 2–13 and 20–22).

The transmission into other prices had been slower than anticipated. Agents’ contacts expected food inflation around 4% at year-end against an April expectation of 6–7%. Hedges, inventories and squeezed margins could delay a later rise. Firms’ expected annual wage growth remained at 3.4%, broadly steady since before the conflict. Some pay indicators suggested private wage pressure closer to 3½% than the headline 2.9% regular earnings measure. The question was whether highly visible energy and food bills would arrive just before agreements for 2027. At the same time second-quarter GDP had risen 0.4%, and stronger July data lifted the staff update for third-quarter growth from 0.1% to 0.4%. Vacancies and hiring still pointed to slack, but some indicators suggested it had stopped increasing. Sampling problems in the labour-force survey warranted care in interpreting unemployment (paragraphs 9–17 and 23–26).

Quoted two-year fixed mortgages cost about 95 basis points more than before the conflict. Nearly all respondents to the market survey closing on 4 September expected a hold. The market curve later rose and indicated a peak around 4.9% by the end of 2027. That comparison spans different information dates and includes risk premia. For most members, transmission into actual borrowing rates supported waiting. Others doubted that globally driven premia would persist without an increase in Bank Rate. Among the hold voters, Bailey and Lombardelli described a strengthening case for a hike if the disruption continued. Dhingra and Taylor placed greater weight on slack, earlier tightening and weak evidence of feedback (paragraphs 6–8, 26–30 and members’ views).

The quantitative tightening decision requires careful accounting. On 16 September the monetary-policy gilt stock was £488 billion. The Bank would retain £120 billion of the longest bonds as backing for banknotes, leaving £368 billion to unwind. Of that, £222 billion was expected to mature and £146 billion to be sold. Annual sales of £20 billion alongside those maturities implied an average annual decline of £46 billion, with completion expected in 2034. Passive maturities, active sales and reassignment of the backing asset have different implications for the issuance investors must absorb. Treating the whole change in the reported stock as open-market sales would substantially overstate the flow (paragraphs 39–46 and 50–52).

Staff estimated that gilt term premia had risen around 200 basis points since quantitative tightening began in 2022, with roughly 20–30 points attributable to the unwind. Those are model-based estimates, not an announcement-day move. The committee preferred a known schedule, revisitable if Bank Rate alone proved insufficient to meet target or markets became severely distressed. A possible implementation through sales to the government was under consideration with the Treasury and Debt Management Office. The implementation decision was still open, with Bank auctions to pause pending details by April 2027. The vote fixed a portfolio objective and planned pace while leaving the execution route unresolved. A market study of this day therefore needs to distinguish near-term rate guidance from duration supply and changes in how gilt sales might be conducted (paragraphs 31–44 and 50–52).

questions.question: Which part of the yield curve responded to Bank Rate guidance, and which to the gilt plan?
questions.detail: Measure meeting-dated sterling forwards, long gilt yields and maturity-matched swaps around the same publication time. Compare gilts with different exposure to the portfolio plan and control for global duration moves. The decisions were issued together, so a single long-yield change cannot identify either effect. Evidence specific to gilt–swap spreads or particular maturities can help distinguish channels, subject to spillovers.

questions.question: How much duration would investors actually absorb under the new schedule?
questions.detail: Reconcile the £488 billion initial stock with the £120 billion set aside, the maturities and the remaining planned sales. Use security-level duration, redemption dates and expected government financing to estimate a range of private-sector exposures. Treat sales to government as conditional on the implementation decision. A stock reduction, a private sale and an equivalent amount of duration risk are three different quantities.

questions.question: Was slower food-price pass-through evidence of weaker pricing power or a delay from hedging?
questions.detail: Compare producers with similar energy exposure and demand but different contract expiry dates. Track input costs, realised selling prices and margins as protection expires. Include agricultural commodity shocks and weather separately. If prices accelerate primarily as hedges roll off even in sectors with weak sales, the mechanism differs from a broader recovery in markups coinciding with stronger demand and less labour slack.
